what_its_for: This medicine helps control blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. It works in three ways: empagliflozin helps your kidneys remove extra sugar through your urine, linagliptin helps your body release more insulin after meals, and metformin helps your body use insulin better and reduces the amount of sugar your liver makes.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth with food, usually in the morning, to reduce stomach upset. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, break, or chew it. Drink plenty of water throughout the day. Keep taking this medicine even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your current diabetes medicines and how well your kidneys are working. Common doses include tablets containing empagliflozin 10 mg or 25 mg, linagliptin 5 mg, and metformin 1000 mg. Most people take one tablet once daily in the morning with food. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container, away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. If your medicine expires or you no longer need it, ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol, as this can lower blood sugar and increase the risk of a rare but serious side effect called lactic acidosis. Avoid skipping meals, as this can cause low blood sugar, especially if you take other diabetes medicines. Tell your doctor before having any surgery, CT scan, or MRI with contrast dye, as you may need to temporarily stop this medicine. Avoid becoming dehydrated — drink enough fluids, especially in hot weather or during exercise.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: unusual muscle pain, trouble breathing, stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or feeling cold — these could be signs of lactic acidosis (a rare but serious condition); signs of a urinary tract infection such as burning when you urinate, frequent urination, or pelvic pain; signs of a genital yeast infection such as itching, redness, or unusual discharge; signs of a rare but serious genital infection called Fournier's gangrene (pain, tenderness, redness, or swelling in the genital or rectal area, along with fever); very low blood sugar (shakiness, dizziness, sweating, confusion, or fainting); signs of diabetic ketoacidosis such as nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, tiredness, or trouble breathing even if your blood sugar is not very high; or if you have signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing.
when_it_works: Metformin usually starts lowering blood sugar within a few days, but it may take 2 to 4 weeks to see the full effect. Empagliflozin and linagliptin also begin working within a few days. Your doctor will check your blood sugar and A1C levels (a 3-month average of your blood sugar) regularly to see how well the medicine is working. It may take up to 3 months to see your best A1C results.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Your doctor will monitor your kidney function more closely, as this medicine may not be suitable if your kidneys are not working well. You may also be at higher risk for dehydration and low blood pressure. Kidney problems: This medicine should NOT be used if your kidneys are severely impaired (eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73m²). Your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment. Liver problems: This medicine is generally not recommended if you have severe liver problems. Pregnancy: Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant, especially during the second and third trimesters, as it may harm your unborn baby. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in children.
